scope: grade 6 NY-6.NS.4 to NS.8 and NY-6.G.3 -- additional evidence

added.quote: Determine the location of points P, X, and Y
Plot a point on the number line to represent the value -3.2.

g6-2023-002.note: The existing Warm-up only primes the idea; these two show Lesson 2 going on to ask students to name the values of lettered points on a number line and then assessing a negative non-integer (-3.2) in the Cool-down -- the item's exact task.

added.quote: The least common multiple of 6 and 8 is 24.

added.lessonTitle: Using Common Multiples and Common Factors
added.quote: including the greatest common factor and least common multiple

g6-2023-013.note: Adds the activity where 'least common multiple' is first named and defined, and shows the idea still being worked two lessons later in Lesson 18, so the Cool-down citation is not the whole span.

added.quote: introduced to the absolute value of a number as its distance from zero
A city that has an elevation of -17 meters is closer to sea level

g6-2023-017.note: Adds where absolute value is first built as distance from zero (Lesson 6 Activity 1) and, earlier still, the Lesson 1 Cool-down that already asks which elevation is closer to sea level -- the item's exact question, two weeks before the placement.

added.activity: Finding Distances in a Coordinate Plane
added.quote: use of the general two-dimensional distance formula is not expected
Here are the coordinates for four polygons.

g6-2023-021.note: Shows that the side-length work is actually developed in Lesson 14, where the curriculum explicitly restricts itself to horizontal and vertical distances, and that Lesson 15 first has students plot polygons from a list of coordinates.

added.quote: 14 is less than 21, so -14 is also less than -21

added.activity: Rational Numbers on a Number Line
added.quote: Decide whether each inequality statement is true or false

g6-2023-038.note: Adds the activity that surfaces the exact misconception the item's distractors test (that -14 < -21 because 14 < 21) and the follow-up where students judge inequality statements about negatives.

added.lessonTitle: Interpreting Points in a Coordinate Plane
added.quote: introduces the idea of vertical difference on the coordinate plane
What is the distance between points A and B

g6-2024-004.note: Adds the Lesson 13 activity that first introduces vertical difference in the coordinate plane -- the item is a purely vertical distance -- and the Cool-down where that distance is assessed.

added.quote: the same distance from 0 on the number line are called opposites

g6-2024-018.note: Adds the activity where 'opposites' is defined as same distance from 0, which is the idea the existing Cool-down citation assesses. Nothing else in the unit works the -(-x) notation, so only one citation was added.

added.quote: If a point has a positive y -coordinate, in which quadrants could it be?
Plot the point (-3, 2) . Label it E

g6-2024-026.note: Shows the sign-and-quadrant reasoning the item needs being worked in Lesson 11, three lessons before the reflection language of the placement, and assessed by plotting signed coordinates in the Lesson 14 Cool-down.

added.activity: Rational Numbers on a Number Line
added.quote: students plot positive and negative numbers on a horizontal number line
Write a sentence to compare the two points shown on the number line.

g6-2024-029.note: Adds the activity where students plot signed numbers and evaluate position claims, and the Lesson 4 Cool-down that asks for a sentence comparing two points -- the sentence form the item's answer choices take.

added.quote: The greatest common factor of 30 and 18 is 6.
how you know that it is the largest possible number of boxes

g6-2024-043.note: Adds where 'greatest common factor' is first named and where students must justify that a number is the largest possible -- the justification the item demands when it asks whether the claim is correct.

added.quote: Write the coordinates of each labeled point.
What is the distance between points C and D?

g6-2024-045.note: Adds where reading and writing coordinates is built (Lesson 11), which the item explicitly requires in its answer, alongside the Cool-down that assesses the distance itself.

added.lessonTitle: Interpreting Points in a Coordinate Plane
added.quote: Label each point in the coordinate plane with the letter that represents its coordinates.
Name two coordinates that could be the landing points of her two arrows.

g6-2025-003.note: Adds the Lesson 11 Cool-down that assesses naming coordinates in the lower quadrants, and the Lesson 13 Warm-up that asks students to match lettered points to ordered pairs -- the item's exact task, two lessons after the placement.

added.lessonTitle: Using Negative Numbers to Make Sense of Contexts
added.activity: Notice and Wonder: It Comes and Goes
added.quote: introduce positive and negative numbers in the new context of money and inventory

added.lessonTitle: Using Negative Numbers to Make Sense of Contexts
added.quote: What does -25 mean in this situation?

g6-2025-031.note: Adds where the money-and-inventory context is first introduced and where students first interpret a specific negative amount, so the entry covers the whole of Lesson 5 rather than only its Cool-down.

added.quote: Find all of the factors of 28 and 12.

added.lessonTitle: Using Common Multiples and Common Factors
added.quote: the side length, in feet, of the largest possible tile she could use

g6-2025-039.note: Adds where 'greatest common factor' is defined and practised on bare number pairs, and shows the same idea reappearing in a Lesson 18 tiling problem.

added.quote: How far away are they from the y -axis?
Students must determine from the information given that each grid square has length 2.

g6-2025-044.note: Adds the activity that builds horizontal distance from the y-axis and the Lesson 15 maze, where students must work out the scale of a grid square -- the item's 'each unit represents 1 foot'.

added.lessonTitle: Comparing Numbers and Distance from Zero
added.quote: A submarine is at an elevation of -100 feet (100 feet below sea level)
Label each point on the number line with the name of the city

g6-2026-002.note: Shows that reading signed elevations off a number line keeps recurring after the placement: Lesson 7's Warm-up glosses -100 feet as 100 feet below sea level, and the Lesson 3 Cool-down uses the item's exact figure of cities labelled on a number line.

added.activity: Finding Distances in a Coordinate Plane
added.quote: Find the distance between each pair of points.
find horizontal and vertical distances between coordinates in a puzzle

g6-2026-005.note: Adds the Lesson 14 activity where finding the distance between two points is actually taught, and the Lesson 15 maze where horizontal and vertical distances are practised before the Cool-down assesses them.

added.quote: What is the opposite of -3.2?

g6-2026-008.note: Adds the Cool-down that assesses the opposite of a signed number directly. Lesson 2 Activity 2 is the only other place opposites are developed, and it is already the existing citation, so nothing further was added.

added.quote: The least common multiple of 6 and 8 is 24.

added.lessonTitle: Using Common Multiples and Common Factors
added.quote: A florist orders sunflowers every 6 days and daisies every 4 days.

g6-2026-017.note: Adds the Lesson 17 activity that states the least common multiple of 6 and 8 is 24 -- literally this item's numbers and answer -- and the Lesson 18 Cool-down that asks students to recognise this problem type from a repeating-schedule story.

added.quote: Which temperature has a smaller absolute value? Explain how you know.

added.lessonTitle: Comparing Numbers and Distance from Zero
added.quote: One partner will use 2 numbers and 1 symbol to write a true statement.

g6-2026-020.note: Adds the one undamaged place the curriculum asks which number has the smaller absolute value, plus the optional partner game where students write comparison statements using both inequality symbols and absolute value.

added.quote: How are the coordinates the same? How are they different?
How far did he walk from his starting point to his ending point?

g6-2026-033.note: Adds where students compare how two points' coordinates are alike and different -- the reasoning the item's answer choices need -- and the Lesson 15 maze where a distance is found from start and end coordinates.

added.quote: students connect a visual number line representation of positive and negative numbers

added.activity: Rational Numbers on a Number Line
added.quote: Plot the numbers -2, 4, -7, and 10 on the number line.

g6-2026-039.note: Adds the activity that connects the number line to inequality symbols in a temperature context, matching the item's context, and the follow-up where students plot signed numbers before comparing them.
